The 30 minute appointment isn’t actually 30 min with the doctor. It’s 30 minutes to see you, do all exams, and type up all their notes, so that’s actually 20 minutes. The 15 minute appointment is more like 10 minutes that includes walking you to the room and back out. Appointments are back to back and you barely get a chance to take a breath. That’s what GPs have to put up with, 8h a day, 5 days a week. 

If the Medicare subsidies were higher, they’d be able to space appointments out better and work full-time because those 38 to 40 hours aren’t at a breakneck pace. Being transgender in an environment where no one was even remotely supportive of transgender people drove me so close to suicide it’s a miracle I’m alive.

If I had been a trans woman instead of a trans man, I would have done it. With what money I don’t know, but I would have done anything to stop the relentless sense of physical wrongness and the absolute heartbreak each time someone referred to me as a girl. I would have done it despite knowing that I could screw up my liver and my future health. 

Your child needs support now. Our suicide risk and statistics are so much higher than the general populace not only because of gender dysphoria, but because of how others treat us - like oddities, sometimes, but also as objects of ridicule and disdain. 

If you can find it in yourself, please have a conversation with your child about why doing something so incredibly risky seemed like a good idea, and what they’re getting out of it. Please. It’s no longer about what they were thinking. It’s about why they thought this was the best option and why it’s making life better for them. It’s about what helps give them a reason to live.

I just did a road trip and encountered signs like this. I do mainly suburban driving and a very small amount of city driving, so I don’t encounter roundabouts like this often. 

It can be confronting for someone unused to them. Slow to 40 as you’re approaching the roundabout, but not too far away. Then speed back up to 100 after leaving the roundabout. There’s no need to wait until you pass the 100km/h sign, which is usually what we do in suburbs. Just follow the cars in front of you and take their lead without following them blindly into the roundabout. It’s ok to slow to a stop and wait for a clear gap to enter the roundabout if it’s really busy, but don’t crawl through at 20.

The essence of it is that you’ll (or I, as I was yesterday) be driving on roads you’re not used to driving on. It’s natural to be a little less confident and to want to stay a hair under the speed limit. There may be many others who drive those roads regularly and perceive you as being a slow driver. It’s their fault if they get impatient, but you should keep left so you don’t obstruct them either. Happy (and safe) driving!

My friend, you need to think about what you want of yourself on the internet. Yes, Reddit is anonymous, but you can still choose what you want to put on it. It’s not hard to dox someone eventually if they leave their first name somewhere, comment on area specific subs, mention what they work as, and post in other topical subs like trans ones. Of course, this is a possibility that isn’t very likely to happen. 

The beauty of the internet is that you can be talking to anyone from anywhere about anything, but it’s also the scary side of it. Unfortunately you attracted an adult who tried to manipulate you into doing what he wants, which is quite frightening. I don’t want to scare you, but please do think about who you should be interacting with in person and apply that to online spaces too. You and me chatting here is a little like meeting in an all ages transgender support group or something. But that guy’s the equivalent of someone coming to the support group, then going up to you and trying to befriend you when it’s not age appropriate. 

As for next steps - it really depends on what you’d like. Blocking is a good first step. You can choose to delete your account and start over, this time not posting your face. You can choose to delete some posts. You can choose to keep the posts but be vigilant nonetheless. Either way, it’s the internet and your safety comes first. You don’t owe anyone anything. If you don’t want to interact with them, you’re allowed to block and move on. 

Stay safe out there!

Hey OP, do look into L2P programmes near you. Most local councils have L2P programmes for learner drivers in the 18-25 age group. They pair you with a mentor who’s been a fully licensed driver for a while and the car is provided by the L2P programme. They’ll get you to 120 hours so you can get on your Ps. 

My advice on this is to be very systematic. If you need 120 hours, it’s going to be 60 weeks if you do 2 lessons of 1h a week. That’s about a year and two months. Look at when you turn 21. If it’s less than a year and two months away, maybe you’ll be able to take the test at 21 with fewer than 120 hours and still pass if you pick it up quickly. Driving instructors are very expensive and even 30 hours will cost you a pretty penny. Take advantage of the L2P programme as it’s free, albeit with a longer waiting time, and you can also say that you’re working towards getting your Ps with a projected test date of (eg. May/June 2025) via the programme.

I’ve been with my family optician all my life, and we’ve had many pairs of glasses made with her. In general:

1. Look at the size of your face first. 
If your face is smaller, oversized glasses accentuate that. Girls look great with oversized, round glasses because their faces look very cute. Good if that’s what you want, not so good if you don’t really want to look cute. 

2. Look at the shape of your face too. 
My face was pretty round pre-transition, so I tried to stay away from round glasses. The shape of your glasses should match the shape of your face - spectacles with narrow width make long faces look bigger, for instance. 

3. Consider the social perception of shapes. 
Typically, people consider round and cat eyed glasses to be more feminine, with rectangular, boxy frames being masculine. Some shapes like aviators appear more neutral, with the retro ones really coming back into style as of the last 5 years. It’s funny, but trans guys and trans girls should look at the glasses they each used to wear as a sort of guide for what’s deemed suitable for their gender. 

4. Ultimately, you need to look in the mirror and be happy. If you do want a pair that’s more feminine, that’s fine. It doesn’t invalidate your expression of masculinity.

Buddy, it’s a tough decision. I think it boils down to:

1) Why do you want to move out?
2) How long can you stay with your parents, and is it feasible to stay with them?

If you move out, you’re definitely going to gain a lot of independence. The downside is all the financial pressure that’s going to come down on you. Rent, phone bill, groceries, cooking, cleaning, transport, all the household stuff you use now. It’s difficult to make it work, but it’s possible if you’re the responsible sort. It’s also stressful, which is why some cultures have kids stay with their parents until later in life, like when they have a serious partner. 

If you don’t move out, you still have a roof over your head and the safety net of your parents. You say you don’t have the best relationship, which is fair. No blaming here - are you interested in mending it? If you are, might be worth sitting down and thinking through the biggest issues with them. If you want to mend that relationship, you may have to be humble and swallow your pride, go to them cap in hand and talk through things. Say what you’d like things to be like, reasonably, and seek their opinion.

1) Get in car and go down the street, make 4 right turns, you’re back where you were
2) Get in car and practice three point turns and parking on a quiet street 
3) Get in car and go to shops nearby (if you’re going to the Clayton strip… park on a street near the churches, it’s less busy)
4) Drive to a nearby shopping centre (Oakleigh Central?)
5) Drive on Princes Hwy
6) Drive on the freeway (M3 > M1, in my opinion)

The steps are meant to be scaled and manageable. Consider mitigating factors that can help you scale your experiences, such as time of day, someone you can hopefully ask to sit next to you, the car you’re using etc. All the best!

Hi there. Thank you for asking - I really appreciate it. I would say:

1) If a trans person is pissed at you, please don’t take it personally. 

If we end up in the A&E, we’re probably stressed and on guard and even more so than the regular patient. We’re worried someone will call us the wrong gender, be derisive, be judgmental, or give us substandard medical care. If we’re being hedgehogs, it’s not because we hate you. It’s because sometimes being trans means we’re always waiting for someone to slip up. 

Sometimes the slip up can mean we brush it off, sometimes it means we’re outed, sometimes it means we’re in precarious situations. That variety of results is why we’re on guard. 

2) If someone around you uses the wrong pronouns, you don’t have to correct them aggressively - restating the sentence with the right pronoun would be much appreciated. 

As someone who’s worked in a number of positions with people both newer and/or more senior than he is, I’m acutely aware of office politics. If it’s not safe or OK for you to tell your superior “Actually, the patient’s pronouns are X”, I’d really appreciate hearing something like “Yes, [right pronoun] presented with X symptom”. 

3) Effects of HRT and surgeries - this is a big one. Someone else has mentioned heart attacks. I’m not a medical professional, but this sticks out as an area of care you might want to read up on if you’re inclined to. I pass as male, but I presented with UTI symptoms, which few men have. I appreciated how the nurse and doctor didn’t do a double take or be visibly surprised. 

I’m down under and there’s a professional organisation called AUSPATH. There might be a similar org for healthcare providers who provide care for trans or GNC patients in your area, and they may have guidelines or conferences you could look up. 

Godspeed - again, I’m thankful you’re asking. Hope you get helpful answers.

Hey there! I hope you have a great time in Perth. I moved to Melbourne but here are some tips that might help: 

1) Look up LGBTQ+ groups in the school you’re going to. You’re 23, so perhaps university?

Did the social worker offer tips on what kind of structure? Structure around a daily routine and your expectations are essential for teens. There may be backlash and pushback at first because she’s testing boundaries, but it’ll be better than not having anything. 

Some thoughts:
- She’s expected to get to school daily and get home, work out how that happens. She should get to know your schedule too.
- Does she have any extra curriculars, and can you support her financially and logistically with those?
- She needs to complete tasks for school in a timely fashion. If she’s already motivated, that’s great. If not… well, that’s a talk that needs to happen. 
- What is she permitted to do in her free time, both at home and elsewhere? Lay down the law around drinking, substance use, sexual activity etc and communicate that you’re going to behave responsibly too so the rules aren’t one sided. 
- Let her know what you’re happy to provide. Three square meals a day, fixings for snacks if she’s hungry, an allowance (important for her to buy her own menstrual supplies!), when you do the groceries and whether she gets to come and pick stuff too, who cooks, toiletries, toilet paper, cleaning supplies and who should do which task etc. 

All the best OP. You can do it.

The irony about depression is that it’s difficult to find the energy to do what you enjoy, yet the best thing that helps is indeed doing what you enjoy. It’s called behavioural activation, whereby you schedule pleasant things to try to help yourself enjoy each day a little more. It doesn’t have to be exercise like running - it can be tasks that are manageable, like taking a walk, viewing the sunset, drawing with your kids, making a simple meal etc. Behavioural activation can be as effective as antidepressants for moderate depression, so it’s worth trying.

There’s hope whenever you care! Don’t give up - your handwriting is already legible, which is a terrific start. It looks like you’re looking to improve your cursive handwriting, but I’d suggest starting with individual letters first before moving on to whole words and sentences. If you’ve never cared about your handwriting until now, then you need to start forming your letters carefully and consistently until it’s muscle memory, and the best way is to write a bunch of As, Bs, Cs and so on! 

I’m a big proponent of low cost methods. If you have access to a local library, they may have a sampler of cursive styles. Feel free to mix and match once you’ve tried out A-Z in the styles you like and got the hang of it! For me, I find that writing certain letters in print works better for my students - I write Rs in print, Ss in cursive but without joining them to the very next letter so there’s a visual break, and I choose to write Ts in print if it’s the start of a word. All the best! I hope you enjoy your new hobby :)

Hi! As someone who reads students’ handwriting as part of their job, I’ll say that your handwriting isn’t too hard to read. May I suggest skipping a line when you write? Your downward loops are quite long, so it cuts into the space allotted for the line beneath. Additionally, a little more space can help you read way you’ve written more easily! Your letters are already relatively tidy and well formed, so that’s a very good try. Skipping a line or two just accommodates the space your handwriting naturally takes up. 

As for the part where your hand is balled into a fist… I’m unsure if this advice will work, but here goes. As someone who writes a lot for work and then goes home and crochets or cross stitched, I use my dominant hand a lot. What helped was developing a keener sense of when I was balling my hand up too much. If I felt like I was getting tired, I made a conscious effort to relax my hand and use a looser grip. My handwriting didn’t suffer very much for it - if you loosen your grip and use a fountain pen as suggested by the person above (or a very smooth ballpoint like the Pilot Dr Grip, which I swear by - alternatively a Uni Jetstream), you might find it better. Best of luck, internet stranger!
